lesson.title: Build an ls-style CLI in Rust with clap, tabled and serde
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

goalMatch.note: This code-along builds a Rust CLI app using crates (likely including argument parsing via cargo), which closely matches your goal, though the description doesn't confirm exactly how arguments are hand

sources.title: Build an ls-style CLI in Rust with clap, tabled and serde

steps.title: Create project and parse path argument
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add clap with the derive feature to Cargo.toml, and define a `#[derive(Parser)]` struct with `path: Option<PathBuf>` parsed via `Cli::parse()` in main. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: Derive Parser on the Cli struct

explanations.topic: clap derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Deriving Parser adds the parse method
Passing args through cargo run with --
Generated usage, arguments and options sections

hints: Add clap to Cargo.toml with features = ["derive"] (or run `cargo add clap --features derive`).
Define a struct with a field `path: Option<PathBuf>` and put `#[derive(Parser)]` above it.
Import with `use clap::Parser;` and `use std::path::PathBuf;`, then call `let cli = Cli::parse();` in main.
Run `cargo run -- -h` — the `--` separates cargo's flags from your program's.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the "derive" feature, so #[derive(Parser)] fails to compile
Not importing clap::Parser, so Cli::parse() is not found
Running `cargo run -h`, which shows cargo's help instead of your app's
Using PathBuf without `use std::path::PathBuf`

steps.title: Add version and about metadata
steps.instructions: Annotate your Cli struct in src/main.rs with `#[command(version, about, long_about = "...")]`. Verify with `cargo run -- --version` and `cargo run -- -h`.

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-generates a --version flag from Cargo.toml
Help output picks up the new version flag automatically
long_about text shown in help output
Clap generates CLI boilerplate so you focus on program logic

hints: Clap reads extra metadata from a #[command(...)] attribute placed above the struct, under #[derive(Parser)].
Use #[command(version, about, long_about = "...")]. version comes from Cargo.toml.
Run `cargo run -- --version`; the `--` passes the flag to your program, not cargo.
If help doesn't show long_about, try `-h` vs `--help`: clap shows long_about with --help, and -h falls back to it if no doc comment exists.
common_mistakes: Writing #[clap(...)] or #[command] above derive without importing Parser, or misspelling long_about as longabout.
Forgetting `--` so cargo itself handles --version and prints cargo's version.
Not enabling clap's derive feature (clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }), so #[command] is unknown.
Putting the attribute on main or a field instead of the struct.

steps.title: Default path and check existence
steps.instructions: Default the path with `cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))`, check it with `fs::exists(&path)`, and print "Path does not exist" in red via owo-colors (add the crate). Test with `cargo run -- longpath`.

targets.caption: Red error for a missing path

explanations.topic: cli.path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default PathBuf
Defaulting to the current directory like ls
fs::exists returns a Result<bool>, handled with if let Ok
owo-colors crate for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the debug executable in target/debug

hints: cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>; use unwrap_or to fall back to PathBuf::from(".").
fs::exists(&path) returns a Result<bool>; destructure it with `if let Ok(does_exist) = ...` and handle Err in an else branch.
Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml, import owo_colors::OwoColorize, then call .red() on the message string.
Run `cargo run -- longpath` (note the `--`) to pass a nonexistent path and see the red message.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `--` in `cargo run -- longpath`, so the argument goes to cargo instead of your program.
Not importing the OwoColorize trait, so `.red()` isn't found.
Using Path::exists (returns bool) with `if let Ok(...)`, causing a type mismatch.
Passing `path` by value to fs::exists and then trying to use it later (move error); pass `&path`.
Forgetting to `return` after printing the error, so the program keeps going.

steps.title: List directory entries with get_files
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that iterates `fs::read_dir(path)` and collects each entry's file name, then loop over it in main printing each name and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: New helper that returns the directory's file names
cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: Returning a Vec<String> as a simple first version of get_files
if let Ok(...) around fs::read_dir to skip unreadable directories
file_name().into_string() returns a Result, so unwrap_or supplies a fallback name
Running with no argument defaults to the working directory

hints: Write a separate function that takes a &Path and returns Vec<String>, then call it from main.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)`, loop `for entry in read_dir`, and unwrap each entry with another `if let Ok(file) = entry`.
Get the name with `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` and push it onto the vector.
In main: `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }`, then run `cargo run` with no arguments.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`, which causes unresolved-name errors.
Passing `path` instead of `&path`, which moves a PathBuf when the function expects &Path.
Calling `.unwrap()` on `into_string()` instead of `unwrap_or`, which panics on non-UTF-8 names.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so `push` fails to compile.
Writing `unwrap_or("unknown name")` without `.into()`, which is a &str vs String type mismatch.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into FileEntry
steps.instructions: Add `strum` with derive, define `enum EntryType { File, Dir }` and `struct FileEntry` filled from `fs::metadata` in a `map_data` function. Pretty-print the entries with `{:#?}` and `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Struct that holds each entry's metadata

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata
Using an enum for entry type and strum's Display derive
fs::metadata returns a Result, so use if let Ok
Bug: passing the directory path instead of file.path()
Extracting the mapping into map_data

hints: Define a struct FileEntry with name: String, e_type: EntryType, len_bytes: u64, modified: String, and add #[derive(Debug)] to it.
Add strum with the derive feature, e.g. `cargo add strum --features derive`, then put #[derive(Debug, Display)] on enum EntryType { File, Dir }.
Inside the loop, use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, then push a FileEntry. Set e_type to EntryType::Dir when meta.is_dir() and to File otherwise, and set len_bytes to meta.len().
Return a Vec<FileEntry> from get_files and print it with println!("{:#?}", ...). Move the push logic into a map_data function.
common_mistakes: Passing the directory path to fs::metadata instead of file.path(), so every entry gets the same metadata.
Matching `Some(meta)` instead of `Ok(meta)`; fs::metadata returns a Result.
Naming the field `type`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust. Use e_type.
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)] on FileEntry or EntryType, so {:#?} fails to compile.
Adding strum without the derive feature, so the Display derive is not found.

steps.title: Render a colored table with tabled
steps.instructions: Add the `tabled` crate, derive `Tabled` on your entry struct, build a `Table::new(...)` with `Style::rounded()` and colored columns/rows, rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = ...)]`, and print it with `cargo run`.

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: render structs as ASCII tables
Choosing a table Style (rounded)
table.modify targets columns/rows to add foreground color
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)] attributes

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled) and derive Tabled on FileEntry alongside Debug.
Replace the for-loop with let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path)); then println!("{}", table).
Use table.with(Style::rounded()) and table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN); Rows::first() targets the header row.
Every field type must implement Display for Tabled — implement Display for your entry-type enum if it errors.
common_mistakes: Forgetting #[derive(Tabled)] on FileEntry, so Table::new won't accept the Vec.
Declaring table without mut, so .with/.modify fail to borrow mutably.
Enum field (file/dir type) lacking a Display impl, causing a trait-bound compile error.
Importing Style/Color from wrong paths; in recent tabled they live under tabled::settings.
Leaving the old for-loop printing in place, giving duplicate output.

steps.title: Format modified date with chrono
steps.instructions: Add `chrono` to Cargo.toml and in map_data use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` to convert into `DateTime<Utc>` and format it with `date.format("%a %b %e %Y")`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see dates in the table.

targets.caption: Add the chrono crate to dependencies
Branch on whether the modified time is available
Convert SystemTime into a chrono DateTime
Run cargo run -- src and see dates in the table

explanations.topic: Why chrono: std has no date formatting
Fallback to empty string when modified time unavailable
meta.modified() returns Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> via into()
strftime-style format specifiers

hints: Add chrono to Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add chrono`) and import DateTime and Utc from it.
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>, so match it with `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }`.
Annotate the conversion: `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();`. The type annotation tells `into()` what to produce.
Format with `date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`, then run `cargo run -- src`.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`, which is a reserved keyword. Use `modi` or another name.
Forgetting the `DateTime<Utc>` type annotation, so `into()` cannot infer its target type.
Not importing `chrono::{DateTime, Utc}`, or not adding chrono to Cargo.toml.
Returning a DelayedFormat instead of a String. Call `.to_string()` or use `format!`.
Running `cargo run src` without the `--` separator.

steps.title: Add --json flag with serde
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, derive `Serialize` on your structs (add serde with derive and serde_json), and print `serde_json::to_string(...)` when the flag is set, else print the table. Test with `cargo run -- -j`.

targets.caption: Table printing extracted into its own function
Serialize the file list to a JSON string
Help output now lists the json flag

explanations.topic: A bare bool field isn't a flag until it has #[arg(short, long)]
Why serde (derive) plus serde_json are needed to serialize to JSON
Every nested type (the EntryType enum) must also derive Serialize
unwrap_or supplies a fallback string if serialization fails

hints: Run `cargo run -- --help`: does it list a -j/--json option? If not, check the attribute on your bool field.
The json field needs `#[arg(short, long)]` above it so clap creates both -j and --json.
Add `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` and `serde_json = "1"` to Cargo.toml, then derive Serialize on FileEntry and on EntryType.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Adding `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats it as a positional argument rather than a -j/--json flag.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on the EntryType enum, which gives a 'Serialize is not implemented' compile error.
Adding serde without the "derive" feature, so #[derive(Serialize)] can't be found.
Forgetting `use serde::Serialize;`.
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`: without the `--`, cargo consumes the flag itself.
Passing the PathBuf to print_table and then reusing it, so the move breaks the json branch; call get_files(&path) by reference.
